For fans of extreme metal of the black and evil variety. Sylfaera the Fair Ataraxia ATARAXIA reminds me of a Tarot reading tent at the Renaissance fair. While fits in with all the knights and maidens and turkey legs and horns of ale, it’s still kind of removed, existing in its own ethereal space. Compos Mentis Pale Horizons Is the album just a little excessive? Perhaps, but that’s a lot of Progressive music in a nutshell. More importantly, it’s also confident, and that kind of thing usually comes from a seasoned band with a few albums in their inventory. The right mix of ingredients is definitely here. This includes a wonderful vocalist, dexterous musicians who know how to support the album without overtaking the sound, and a level of complexity that would make any fan of Progressive music turn their head. This stunning debut really has it all. Counting the Stars and Singing our Hearts out April Spring Although the raging vocal screams could cut through feet of metal and stone like a diamond tipped blade, it’s the melody that stands out most on the album. You can totally get lost in them as well, and they make your heart race when they rise. At its most basic level, music is supposed to make you feel good. That’s why so many of us turn to it when we need a boost. After listening to this, the high I feel might last for weeks. Rúin Ováte Overall, this was a good album. It was a bit traditional when it comes to Black Metal and didn’t veer too far from the path of their forefathers but done with a lot of rage and intensity. You could also make out a lot of the bruising riffs, and they didn’t blur together as much as some bands do in the genre. It was a harrowing listening experience. Aion’s Light Blood & Sun This album was definitely outside of my wheelhouse, and I’m surprised how much I enjoyed it. It’s the kind of album that you can play through while enjoying stories over a campfire in the outdoors at night. The serious nature of the vocals might be my favorite part, and the album has lasting power. The Ecstasy of Death Offernat Overall, this was a good album, that saw it branch out from Black Metal into Doom and even other areas. The Progressive and ambient moments were my favorite, but they just weren't featured as prominently as others. I feel like it was just missing one thing, to catapult the album into the stratosphere, but they just didn’t quite grab a hold of it. From Dark Dimensions an Unspeakable Presence Awakens Striken Of all the various vocal styles out there in Metal, shouting is my least favorite. But I didn’t let that color my review. The main issue I have with the album is that it lacks depth. Doom doesn’t need to be exciting necessarily, but if they take it deep, you can feel it. This album sort of just lingers on the surface for much of the time, which is in and of itself a real feeling, but it just failed to move me. Nycta Psychis Urarv This album was totally different than most Black Metal albums. Sure, the base was there, but when they talk about experimenting, they mean throwing caution out the window.  Unconventional and sophisticated? You bet, and I applaud the band’s constitution in not wanting to sound like every other Black Metal band out there. Evil Black Church Estertor Listen, this wasn’t a bad album, but let’s face it…the sound was done, overdone, and overdone again 30 years ago. They have a lot of energy and enthusiasm, and are excellent musicians, but if you are looking for something different, this ain’t your horse Blood Of The Innocent Gomorra “Blood Of The Innocent” is a smart blend of traditional Heavy Metal with Power and Thrash Metal elements. The guitar work of both guitarists is excellent, but that the vocals which stand out Forbidden Forbidden The self-named album is a Thrash Metal album at its base but also crosses boundaries Farewell to All We’ve Lost Orbita From Bandcamp, “ORBITA stand as a new upcoming force in the Italian Dark Doom Metal […] Seasons Crystal Witch Crystal Witch are an American hard rock and blues band originally formed in November 1989 […] Ante Auroram Lamentari This was very complicated album in terms of all of the components the band had to put into place. But you could feel each piece fitting in and locking into place before the next one, and the best thing I can say about it is that they made complexity feel accessible to the listener. A menacing symphony of death. One Last Walk Once Upon a Winter The themes of struggle and eventual acceptance of chaos in your life come through strongly in the music. Since the tenant is that we can’t overcome chaos, and that makes sense, we have to learn to live with it and make peace. Much of the album wallows deep in that process and prods you to work deeper if you want to come out of the shadows. It’s a beautiful but somber reminder of the power of resolve. Worldwide. 24/7. October 18, 2026 On The Turntable Close The Clientele :: Suburban Light It can be difficult to verbalize exactly what autumnal records are capable of eliciting. One thing is undeniable: October and November are the months for The Clientele’s 2000 debut album Suburban Light . Perhaps most impressive, the uninitiated would never detect that such an accomplished record was comprised mostly of a smattering of the band’s earlier 7″ singles from the years prior. Though ideal for any season, the record is an impeccable collection of reveries that paint a viscerally evocative picture of sundown strolls with scattered leaves underfoot. While often overshadowed by the majestic experimentation of his former project’s late work, Mark Hollis harbors its own secrets and surprises, while building upon the work those albums began. As a final testament, it’s a fitting paradox, full of roaring silences and whispering explosions, a collection of whisper-thin abstractions that have been annealed into something durable and concrete. One of the era’s great young singjays, Boyo moves between vocal and dub across twelve tracks, his delivery drifting over heavyweight riddims before disappearing into the mix. Full of swagger yet mellow and unhurried, he rides the bass-heavy arrangements through a thick haze of echo and reverb. Read More Late November :: Autumnal Britfolk Instrumentals (1968-1981) Posted on November 25, 2026 November 21, 2026 The shadows are lengthening, the leaves are falling, the air is getting crisp. That’s right, we’re heading into the latter days of autumn. Maybe the best time of year? One of them, anyway. The season demands a soundtrack, and for some reason, the loosely organized britfolk genre is perfect for these days. So here’s an hour’s worth of instrumentals from the late 1960s to the early 1980s, when giants walked the earth. Trad melodies and rhythms abound, but there are plenty of left-turns, mostly thanks to dedicated iconoclasts like John Martyn, Davey Graham and Michael Chapman. Grab a pint of something dark and rich and settle in. Transmissions :: Beth Orton Posted on November 25, 2026 November 25, 2026 This week on the show, we’re presenting the penultimate episode of our 12th season. And we’ve saved a tremendous talk for this second to last installment: our guest is singer/songwriter Beth Orton. In the mid-’90s, she emerged as a purveyor of electronic folk, working with artists like William Orbit, The Chemical Brothers, and Four Tet. Her latest is The Ground Above. Reviewing it for Aquarium Drunkard, Kyle Lemmon described it as “a free-flowing mixture of electronic funk, spirit walking jazz, and ambient folk.” The Lagniappe Sessions :: Shane Butler Posted on November 24, 2026 November 22, 2026 Shane Butler’s first solo record, Heavy Debt , is due next month, and for this Lagniappe Session he’s pulled together three songs that have been rattling around for a long time. Fugazi’s “I’m So Tired,” a song he first encountered as a kid watching skate videos, Shoes’ homemade pop and a 1979 Soft Boys’ nugget. Miles Davis: Copenhagen Live 1969 Posted on November 24, 2026 November 21, 2026 Miles Davis’ 1969 live ensemble existed in a parallel timeline alongside his studio work – greasing his audience for a future for which they were wholly unprepared. A new 2LP set, Copenhagen Live 1969 , captures the band at its peak, stress-testing then-unreleased Bitches Brew material, tearing it down and reassembling it into some of the most far-out, formless music of Miles’ career. Frank Black :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview Posted on November 24, 2026 November 24, 2026 In 2025, Pixies leader Frank Black took to the road to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his 1994 sophomore LP Teenager of the Year with the same cast of players who recorded the original album. A sprawling double album, it’s held together with the same kind of ramshackle logic that makes The Beatles’ The White Album or The Clash’s London Calling work. Recently, Aquarium Drunkard caught up with Black to discuss revisiting the album. Along the way, he revealed details about a Pixies record in the works, UFOs, the paranormal, and explained his vision of a future rock & roll cult where artists like The Feelies are elevated to the status of saints. Fine :: Jazz Dreams Posted on November 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 For all the creativity Copenhagen’s avant-pop scene can offer, a lot of it had started to hang on its own clichés. Who knew it could be recharged by a blasé attitude and a good old dose of harmonic complexity? Fine’s Jazz Dreams is full of the kind of drowsy virtuosity that once again justifies the hype over that scene’s prolific output; it’s as if you were inhabiting the fantasies of a conservatory student who fell asleep in counterpoint class. Tía Rosa :: Thirteen Automatic Dreams Posted on November 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 Via Mexico City, Thirteen Automatic Dreams is the thrillingly comfy new record by Tía Rosa. Here is some minimalist kosmische with a Latin pop sensibility, a bridge between the noisy regularity of Neu! and the sugared melancholy of balada romántica. It all plays like a lost soundtrack to the Nevada desert of the Nocilla Trilogy , where shoes hang from a lonely poplar, or like Stereolab is being collectively hallucinated from one of those little Durango towns where Jodorowsky liked to film his deranged acid westerns. Sunday Mourners :: A-Rhythm Absolute Posted on November 23, 2026 November 21, 2026 Skirting the edges of canonical post-punk, the debut record by four piece Sunday Mourners is a gripping, youthful art-rock explosion. There are distinct flashes tapping into Chairs Missing -era jagged melodicism here, VU at their most intractable jamming there (the twelve minute “Darling” a prime example). Above all, A-Rhythm Absolute is a downright lively listen, hitting all of the spirited guitar-centric benchmarks to make the listener a reinvigorated believer in the state of such a modern landscape. Happy Thanksgiving :: Doug Sahm And Friends – Austin, TX 1972 Posted on November 21, 2026 November 21, 2026 Tradition runs rampant around Thanksgiving: generations of old recipes, football, Alice’s Restaurant, and, of course, a parade of balloons shutting down NYC. Yr Knives :: Begin Yr Singing Posted on November 20, 2026 November 20, 2026 On a recent episode of Vish Khanna’s Kreative Kontrol podcast, Douglas McCombs explained that music his his primary social activity. With Chicago’s Yr Knives, he adds yet another group to the mix.
